{{Short description|American thunderstorm prediction index}}
[[File:Supercell Composite April 27, 2011.png|alt=A map of the United States, with contours in blue representing the SCP and black tornado tracks representing EF5-rated tornadoes|thumb|The supercell composite index on [[2011 Super Outbreak|April 27, 2011]], overlaid with tracks of [[Enhanced Fujita scale|EF5]]-rated tornadoes (in black)]]
The '''Supercell Composite Parameter''', often abbreviated as '''SCP''', is a multi-parameter index used by the [[Storm Prediction Center]] that outlines areas of the [[United States]] where the development of [[Supercell thunderstorm|supercell thunderstorms]] is favorable.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mesoscale Parameters |url=https://www.weather.gov/source/zhu/ZHU_Training_Page/convective_parameters/Sounding_Stuff/MesoscaleParameters.html |access-date=2026-05-04 |website=[[National Weather Service]]}}</ref> The parameter uses [[convective available potential energy]], [[storm relative helicity]] and [[vertical wind shear]] to determine specific areas.<ref>{{Cite web |date=August 5, 2005 |title=Climatology of the Supercell Composite Parameter (1979–2004) |url=https://caps.ou.edu/reu/reu05/finalpapers/Smith-finalpaper.pdf |access-date=May 4, 2026 |website=[[Oklahoma University]] |page=2}}</ref> A value of 1 indicates a normal atmosphere while values above two are conducive for supercells.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2017 |title=Utility of Severe Weather Parameters and Indices |url=https://www.weather.gov/media/crp/Severe_Weather_Parameters_Tinsley_2017.pdf |access-date=May 4, 2026 |website=[[National Weather Service]] |pages=28-29}}</ref>

== Equation ==
Two equations can be used to conclude the supercell composite for an area:<ref name=":0" />{{Blockquote|text=SCP = ({{sfrac|MUCAPE|1000 J/Kg^-1}}) x ({{sfrac|0-3 km SRH|150 m^2s-^2}}) x ({{sfrac|BRN denominator|40 m^2s-^2}})}}{{Blockquote|text=SCP = ({{sfrac|MUCAPE|1000 J/Kg^-1}}) x ({{sfrac|Effective shear|20 m^2s-^2}}) x ({{sfrac|Effective SRH|50 m^2s-^2}})}}
